title: Valid Anagram
description: Two strings are anagrams iff their character counts match. One Map, increment for s, decrement for t — all zero at the end means anagram. O(n).

notes: Length check first — different lengths cannot be anagrams, and it lets us skip a final zero-check.
Single Map: +1 walking s, -1 walking t. If any count goes negative, t has a char s did not have.
Space is O(1) because the alphabet is fixed; sorting both strings is O(n log n) — fine in interviews but slower.

questions.q: Why is the length check at the top important?
options: Different lengths cannot be anagrams, and skipping it would force a final scan for non-zero counts
Pure microoptimization with no semantic impact

questions.q: What does it mean if a counter goes BELOW zero during the t scan?
options: t is a prefix of s
t contains a character that s did not — not an anagram

questions.q: Why is the space complexity considered O(1) here?
options: The Map is reused across calls
The alphabet is bounded, so the Map has a fixed maximum size independent of n
It is not — it is O(n)

exercises.prompt: Fill in the single-pass counter approach. The early-exit on negative is what keeps it O(n).

blanks.hint: strict inequality — bail when lengths differ
negative count means t has an extra character

L3.prompt: Write `isAnagram(s, t)` using one Map of character counts (O(n) time). Log `isAnagram("anagram", "nagaram")` then `isAnagram("rat", "car")`.
hints: Increment for s, decrement for t — return false the moment any count goes negative.
Equal length plus no negatives means counts balanced to zero everywhere.
